item.title: Carney says competition, prices and service key for telecom sector
item.description: Prime Minister Mark Carney says more competition, lower prices and better service will be key to any decision regarding the telecom sector.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: SHENZHEN — Prime Minister Mark Carney says more competition, lower prices and better service will be key to any decision regarding the telecom sector. The prime minister made the comments in China where he is attending the APEC summit after he was asked about Quebecor Inc.’s takeover offer for Telus Corp. It’s a proposed deal that would reduce the number of players in Canada’s wireless market, which is already dominated by just a handful of large telecommunication companies. Carney declined to comment directly on the proposal, but said that under certain circumstances and depending on the market structure, an oligopoly situation can lead to more competition with fewer players, though he didn’t elaborate further. Aidan Hollis, an economics professor at the University of Calgary, said in an interview that in general, more industry players leads to greater competition, but that is not always the case. “If you had a really inefficient competitor, that inefficient competitor might end up with a very small market share and potentially if they merge, you get a more efficient competitor who then is able to basically be a more effective competitor in the rest of the market,” he said. If a merger doesn’t lead to greater efficiencies, Hollis said “What you could generally expect is as the market becomes more concentrated with fewer firms, there’s less need to compete aggressively by lower prices or a better service.” Carney said the objective will always be the best service for Canadians at the most competitive prices today and in the future. Telus, which is reviewing the unsolicited Quebecor offer, has said there would be serious regulatory issues with the bid that it also says undervalues the company. Hollis said it is not obvious the deal would be a pro-competition merger. “A merger between two of the four major players would probably not be likely to lead to any substantial increase in efficiency that would result in lower prices,” he said. Quebecor president and CEO Pierre Karl Péladeau has said he and Telus counterpart Victor Dodig are slated to meet next Monday to discuss next steps. Péladeau has touted Quebecor as a fourth national carrier since his company acquired Freedom Mobile in 2023, as part of a deal associated with the larger takeover of Shaw by Rogers Communications Inc. Some telecommunications analysts have cast doubt that the proposed merger with Telus will be completed, citing concerns about whether it would survive regulatory scrutiny. RBC analyst Drew McReynolds called it a “major surprise,” but said he believes there is a “low probability” of the companies joining forces. “Under the current regulatory environment, the required government approvals of a Quebecor-Telus combination without material remedies appears to us to be a non-starter, while such a combination alongside material remedies would naturally bring into question the combination’s underlying strategic rationale,” McReynolds said in a note on Monday. This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 18, 2026. By Daniel Johnson

item.title: Minister says discussions with Meta 'confidential' following reports of possible deal
item.description: Culture Minister Marc Miller says he won’t talk about any discussions the government has had with Meta about restoring news content to the company’s platforms in Canada.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: OTTAWA — Culture Minister Marc Miller says he won’t talk about any discussions the government has had with Meta about restoring news content to the company’s platforms in Canada. A day after Politico reported the company and the government were close to a deal before trade talks with the United States collapsed in August, Miller said today the discussions with Meta are confidential. Citing an unnamed official, Politico said Meta put forward a proposal to stop blocking news content in Canada, pursue commercial deals with publishers and fund two positions at the Canadian Journalism Collective. In exchange, Politico said, the deal would have given Meta an exemption under the Online News Act, which requires Meta and Google to compensate news publishers for the use of their content. Politico reported the proposal was part of the wider U.S.-Canada trade negotiations that Canada shut down in August after accusing the White House of demanding last minute changes that threatened Canada’s sovereignty. After the Online News Act became law in 2023, Meta blocked news content in Canada while Google received an exemption after agreeing to pay $100 million to Canadian news outlets. This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 18, 2026. Anja Karadeglija, The Canadian Press

item.title: Metro CEO says winning back consumers a ‘priority’ after labour strike dented results
item.description: A six-month-long labour strike at Metro’s Laval, Que., fresh produce distribution centre dented the grocery retailer’s fourth-quarter results, as many consumers opted to shop elsewhere.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: MONTREAL — A six-month-long labour strike at Metro’s Laval, Que., fresh produce distribution centre dented the grocery retailer’s fourth-quarter results, as many consumers opted to shop elsewhere. “Our contingency plan ensured continuity, but certainly affected the business,” Marc Giroux said during his first earnings conference call as Metro’s new chief executive officer on Wednesday. “It created a lot of turbulence and affected freshness, assortment and store, and our ability to compete.” Workers returned to work on Sept. 27, the first day of Metro’s fiscal 2027. The strike cost the grocer an estimated $42 million in incremental direct expenses in the fourth quarter, Metro said in a release on Wednesday. It estimates a $132-million hit in fiscal 2026 due to the strike. “The strike is now over, and the team are now focused on rebuilding our sales,” said the CEO, who also took the helm on Sept. 27. Giroux said the Laval distribution centre is “back in shape,” while a multi-week plan remains underway for a gradual recovery for stores. Metro reported it earned $201.9 million or 97 cents per diluted share for the quarter ended Sept. 26. The result was lower, compared with a profit of $217 million or $1.00 per diluted share in the same quarter last year. On an adjusted basis, Metro earned 97 cents per diluted share compared with an adjusted profit of $1.13 per diluted share a year ago. Sales for the quarter totalled $5.18 billion, up from $5.11 billion in the same quarter last year. Its food same-store sales fell 1.9 per cent. Bringing back consumers and driving up sales are the “immediate priority,” Giroux said. The company has launched marketing campaigns and intensified its promotional offerings to attract shoppers. Those efforts come as high gas and food prices continue to eat into household budgets -- pushing shoppers to remain value-centric and search for deals. For fiscal 2027, Giroux said the focus remains on expanding Metro’s discount banners Food Basics and Super C. Meanwhile, Metro’s pharmacy unit was a bright spot, as more consumers opt for generic weight-loss drugs. Pharmacy same-store sales rose 5.5 per cent, boosted by a 6.5 per cent increase in prescription drugs sales and a 3.1 per cent increase in front-store sales. “Pharmacy remains a strong growth engine for Metro,” Giroux said. The company plans to open three new pharmacies and renovate 31 existing stores. This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 18, 2026. By Ritika Dubey

item.title: How the Anthropic IPO stacks up against SpaceX
item.description: The Anthropic IPO is expected to price on Wednesday. The AI lab stands to be the second-biggest U.S. initial offering on record, after SpaceX’s record IPO in June.
item.dc:creator: Reuters Staff
item.content:encoded: The Anthropic IPO is expected to price on Wednesday. What are would-be buyers getting? The AI lab stands to be the second-biggest U.S. initial offering on record, after SpaceX’s record IPO in June. And like SpaceX, an Elon Musk company that sends rockets into space and develops AI models, valuations look stretched, if not quite to the same degree. At the US$1.4 trillion valuation that has been bandied about by bankers in recent weeks, Anthropic would trade at 40 times its sales over the last 12 months. When SpaceX went public at a roughly US$1.8 trillion valuation, it carried a multiple of roughly 92 times revenue in the previous 12 months. That is many times the multiples that other big AI players trade at. Amazon trades at 3.5 times its trailing 12 months sales and Alphabet at 7.3 times, according to LSEG data. But growth is one of the scarcest values in the market and there are signs that once again investors will be willing to pay up. Institutional demand has been strong, Reuters has reported, and in an echo of the SpaceX offering, retail traders are rushing to get shares - even if many analysts and portfolio managers are skeptical. “We wouldn’t be a buyer at this level. We’ll look for drawdowns post the debut and see what we find,” said Tom Hulick, CEO at Strategy Asset Managers, whose firm has some indirect exposure to Anthropic through a growth equity fund. Shares of AI-linked companies have been pressured in recent months by concerns about whether investments are paying off in increased productivity. Rising interest rates are making projects costlier and harder to finance, while the prospect of increased government regulation is hitting sentiment. Add to that the mixed performance of IPOs over the years, especially large ones at high valuations, and there is some doubt about what will happen when Anthropic hits the market on Thursday. “This is the single fastest-growing company of all time. It’s like investing in the stock of Michael Jordan when he’s just starting out,” said Eric Schiffer, chairman of The Patriarch Organization, a Los Angeles-based family office. “But newly-listed companies are volatile in the early stages. And that’s not going to be any different here.” Structural issues could pressure early performance. Anthropic’s IPO lock-up provisions allow certain employees and insiders to sell portions of their holdings from the first trading day, with further staggered releases tied to earnings announcements. Co-founders, who own a total 10 per cent stake, can transfer up to 29 per cent of their holdings after 180 days, with the rest unlocking after a year. By comparison, SpaceX’s lock-up structure was more restrictive for CEO Elon Musk, who owned just under half of the company and is barred from selling his shares for a year, with no early-release provisions. SpaceX’s shares are trading above their IPO price but below the price they opened at in June. How Anthropic’s shares trade could shape the outlook for other blockbuster IPOs, especially rival OpenAI’s, which is expected to go public as soon as next year. “Where the rubber meets the road is the first earnings after the IPO. That’s where you oftentimes see companies fall back,” said Edward Best, co-Chair, capital markets at Willkie Farr & Gallagher. --- Reporting by Niket Nishant in Bengaluru; Writing by Sruthi Shankar; Editing by Colin Barr and Arun Koyyur
